How much protein do you need?

Protein advice is usually given per kilogram of body weight. This guide explains the common reference values and why they are only a starting point.

Educational estimates only. Results are not medical advice, a diagnosis, or a treatment plan. Talk to a qualified healthcare professional about your health. Read the full medical disclaimer.

The baseline reference

The US Recommended Dietary Allowance for healthy adults is 0.8 g of protein per kilogram of body weight per day. UK guidance quoted by NHS sources is slightly lower, around 0.75 g per kilogram. These figures are set to meet the needs of most healthy adults, not to optimise performance or body composition.

Why activity changes the picture

People who exercise regularly or do strength training are often discussed as needing more than the baseline, and sports-nutrition sources vary in the ranges they give. The protein needs estimator uses simple educational assumptions of 1.0 to 1.2 g/kg for recreationally active people and 1.2 to 1.6 g/kg for strength or muscle training. They are not official recommendations, and you can see exactly how they are applied.

A worked example

For a person weighing 70 kg: 0.8 g/kg gives 56 g per day; 1.0 to 1.2 g/kg gives 70 to 84 g; 1.2 to 1.6 g/kg gives 84 to 112 g. The estimator does the same arithmetic and converts pounds to kilograms if you prefer.

Who needs individual advice

Needs differ with age, pregnancy, illness and medication. People with kidney disease in particular are often advised to limit protein, so a general calculator is not appropriate for them. Higher intakes are not automatically better, and this site does not recommend supplements.

Putting it together

Use the number as a rough guide to compare against what you eat, not a target to chase. If you are tracking changes in weight or measurements alongside your eating, the weight progress calculator and tracker can help you see trends. A registered dietitian or doctor can give advice tailored to you.
